    #90469. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1743 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    It has been revealed that this process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal problem in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important concern of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an concern that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    According to recent reports, but much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 notes the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an crucial issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    It has been revealed that just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    According to recent reports, and the justices rarely discuss it. In his newly introduced book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    In a recent development, the clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    According to recent reports, caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    In a recent development, the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    Recent findings suggest that there are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Industry observers note that different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a manufacturer based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    It has been revealed that question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    Industry observers note that the Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal problems, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    It has been revealed that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    Sources indicate that the process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that tuscany, 1972.
    • When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • Recent findings suggest that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful newly introduced novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    When Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some major decisions to make.

    Recent findings suggest that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful newly introduced novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    It has been revealed that I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    In a recent development, radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    It has been revealed that sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    According to recent reports, tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    In a recent development, as for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an important role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    There were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a plan, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    The second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    Recent findings suggest that I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    Sources indicate that as I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    Industry observers note that finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a massive challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    Industry observers note that RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    Sources indicate that SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    It has been revealed that but Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    Recent findings suggest that SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    According to recent reports, that noted, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    But I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    It has been revealed that to mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    Seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    Recent findings suggest that on my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    According to recent reports, radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The New York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    #90466. Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1395 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s a whole latest wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases.
    • Recent findings suggest that note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting.
    • Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s a whole latest wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

    Recent findings suggest that note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are latest releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

    M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century.

    This came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

    Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230.

    It has been revealed that when a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

    James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291.

    According to recent reports, in this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

    Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369.

    Set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their new abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

    A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381.

    I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her fresh novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

    Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn.

    Indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419.

    According to recent reports, hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century.

    At the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

    Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century.

    Recent findings suggest that in 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever strategy to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

    Sources indicate that molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a fresh market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses. (Image from Shutterstock).

    It has been revealed that major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses.

    Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises confirmed in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

    Milbank increased the associate salary range from $235,000 to $455,000. In July, it offered special bonuses between $6,000 and $25,000 for associates. Reuters is also reporting pay increases at Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

    Recent findings suggest that cravath’s special bonuses—$11,000 to $40,000—based on class year, exceeded Milbank’s scale. Its year-end bonus scale starts at $15,000 and extends to $115,000, which is a continuation of what the firm and others offered in past years.

    No comments were given by Cravath.

    #90464. What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2417 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v.
    • In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at problem are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    In a recent development, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in Upcoming York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at problem are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    According to recent reports, at issue in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Strategy.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    Sources indicate that according to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    When and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested issue. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this vital issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    This framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the upcoming policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    Yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    In a recent development, next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the fresh policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at issue intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    The use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Strategy. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    Sources indicate that one answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    The U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater New York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    Industry observers note that this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    Thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    In a recent development, this leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    Sources indicate that deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

    Any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

    It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

    So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”.

    Also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

    Sources indicate that the series will star Melissa George, Jamie Sives, and Ashley Storrie, and will be six episodes long. Ed Sellek of Sister Boniface Mysteries is the creator and head writer.

    Filming begins before the end of the year, so stay tuned!

    #90461. 8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1410 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry.
    • In reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar.
    • Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I took up running in 2010. I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry. My partner at the time had been a serious competitive runner and believed I’d be able to just knock out an eight-minute mile.

    In reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I’d managed to reach number six in the UK for over-forties women’s tennis. It has gradually dawned on me that sporting success isn’t the healthy, glossy, happybodymaxx endeavour that shiny people on Instagram would have us all believe.

    Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.

    Andre Agassi, Open: An Autobiography.

    I read Open when I was on the verge of my own tennis-related nervous breakdown (alas not involving crystal meth like Agassi’s), during a heatwave in Nottingham, in a hotel room full of little flies that I’d become convinced were going to bite me and cause such a severe allergic reaction that I would die. The prologue is one of the best pieces of writing I’ve ever encountered: the extraordinary violence of a five-set tennis match, ending with the wounded competitors lying side by side, holding hands.

    Then there’s Agassi’s father’s $10,000 bet (later reduced to $500) that his nine-year-old son could beat Jim Brown, the famous American Football player. The fact that the book was ghostwritten (by the wonderful J. R. Moehringer) gives it an additional layer of weirdness and gothic edge for me.

    Rafael Nadal (with John Carlin), Rafa.

    This is basically an OCD-fest (although officially Nadal does not have this condition) about Rafa being bullied to sporting success by his Uncle Toni. There’s a chilling story about Toni refusing to let seven-year-old Rafa have a replacement bottle of water to teach him a lesson about losing the first one (you don’t need a psychotherapist to make the link with the water bottle shenanigans on court), and another about telling him he must never make himself the center of attention, even when he was the best tennis player in the world.

    Sources indicate that even as an adult, Nadal describes extraordinary anxieties, including the belief that if he makes a small mistake, his mother might die. The contrast between the superhuman control Nadal displays on the tennis court and the terrifying lack of control he feels everywhere else is what makes this such a disturbing and compelling memoir.

    Serena Williams (with Daniel Paisner), My Life: Queen of the Court.

    There’s a brilliant scene in the incredible Teddy Perkins episode of Atlanta where Teddy, played by Donald Glover, does a roll-call of famous fathers who have abused their children towards greatness. He mentions Joe Jackson, Tiger Woods’s father and Richard Williams.

    Like Andre Agassi’s father, Richard Williams was seemingly determined to create a tennis champion, trying the sport with his older daughters before it finally stuck with his youngest two, Venus and Serena. He would take them to the local tennis courts in Compton with shopping trolleys full of tennis balls. Initially, Venus was the more successful and Serena was determined to beat her own sister so she did not simply become a footnote in Venus’s story.

    Leanne Shapton, Swimming Studies.

    Swimming Studies was actually the book that set me off on my disastrous tennis adventure. It was a single line in it, something about how Leanne Shapton, recovered from her dark sporting childhood, was still placing in “age-group” events. It was those two words, age-group, that made me think perhaps I could resurrect my childhood tennis dreams.

    When I read Swimming Studies, I was myself trying to swim seriously, but ended up with breaststroker’s knee—which is odd, as Shapton suffered exactly the same thing. I felt a little like the book was haunting me, and that I was literally absorbing its ailments quasi-gothically.

    Brad Gilbert (with Steve Jamison), Winning Ugly.

    This was basically my bible during the year I played competitive tennis. Actually, that’s wrong. The Inner Game of Tennis was my bible. This was my grimoire. This may be one of the most fun dark books ever written.

    Sources indicate that basically, Brad Gilbert tells you how you can win at tennis (and maybe even life too)—even if you are shit. You do things like turn up early and have a hit on the court with a local coach (impossible when I tried it), then shower, change and arrive late for the match and suggest starting with no warm up. Gilbert has lots of handy hints for ways to deliberately psych out your opponents with chat specifically designed to derail them.

    Adharanand Finn, The Way of the Runner.

    I really loved Finn’s previous book, Running with the Kenyans, which begins with a stirring account of him unexpectedly winning a 5K fun run. After that he goes to Kenya, meets some Big Characters who introduce themselves with their marathon PBs, and becomes himself a more excellent runner. It’s uplifting and inspiring.

    Industry observers note that but this book about Japanese running methods is far darker. Finn begins this one battling injury and exhaustion and then encounters the weird, workaholic training methods of the Japanese, including running with exaggeratedly short strides and accelerated cadence. There was something bleakly joyless about this book compared with the first one, but I still hoovered it up.

    Christopher McDougall, Born to Run.

    Reading Born to Run isn’t like reading a normal book—it’s an era of your life. My heart skips and I get goosebumps just thinking about it. The ecstatic descriptions of people for whom running is both a way of life and a form of transport, and the theories about primal living, squatting and running barefoot, would go on to underpin my philosophy of sport and life for years to come (and still do).

    After reading this book I became a primal forefoot runner. My friend Vybarr Cregan-Reid, author of Footnotes: How Running Makes Us Human, went totally barefoot, despite various broken-glass incidents in British parks. I will never forget the wonderfully compelling romance of Jenn Shelton and Billy “Bonehead” Barnett, and how they would eat pizza and drink Mountain Dew in the middle of their ultras, like running was something even Lana Del Rey could do.

    Oh, how I loved this dark and crazy book that made running seem like part religion and part disco-party where everyone successfully hides their pain.

    It has been revealed that W. Timothy Gallwey, The Inner Game of Tennis.

    The Inner Game of Tennis changed my entire life and philosophy, and there’s nothing darker than that. I found myself using it as a way of understanding EVERYTHING. The concept is that you have two selves. Self 1 and Self 2. Self 2 will quietly do things if you just leave it alone, but Self 1 is constantly judging. During my disastrous tennis adventure, I could never really get rid of Self 1 and its constant voicings of my coming glory, imminent failure, place in the rankings, what I’d tell my coach, etc.

    One of the tricks Gallwey recommends is reading the writing on the tennis ball as it comes towards you. I’ve encountered this kind of method in other places too, like reciting your own phone number backwards during a panic attack.

    Another dark sports book I still live by is Steve Peters’s The Chimp Paradox, which has some similar ideas about quieting the crazed ego-animal within. Ultimately, if you can let Self 2 take control, you can enter the mythic space of the Zone or Flow, which is, according to Daniel Kahneman’s incredible book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the most optimal place a human can reach.

    Industry observers note that scarlett Thomas was born in London. She is the author of highly acclaimed contemporary cult novels including The End of Mr. Y, which was longlisted for the Orange Broadband Prize for Fiction; Oligarchy; The Seed Collectors; PopCo; The Sleepwalkers; The Runner; and the Worldquake series of middle grade books. Her novels have sold over half a million copies worldwide and been translated into twenty-six languages. Scarlett is professor of creative writing and contemporary fiction at the University of Kent. Find out more at ScarThomas.com.

    #90460. The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2722 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session.
    • Recent findings suggest that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review.
    • Industry observers note that on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session. It also decided an interim docket case on border wall construction in southwestern Texas, granting the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to continue construction in an apparent 8-1 vote.

    Recent findings suggest that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew. Just over an hour later, Pavatt was executed in Oklahoma.

    According to recent reports, on Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    On Monday, the justices heard argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    According to recent reports, later on Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Major Bend region of southwestern Texas. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

    In a recent development, in Monday’s order list, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists.

    In early October, a high school wrestler in Washington state and her mother came to the Supreme Court’s interim docket and asked the justices to prevent transgender girls from competing against her during this year’s wrestling season. The application has been fully briefed since Oct. 15, but the Supreme Court has not yet taken action. In a Monday letter, the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association asked the court not to intervene, highlighting the passage last week of a ballot initiative in Washington that aims to prevent “biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities that have separate classifications for male and female students” at K-12 schools.

    While speaking to the Federalist Society on Thursday, Justice Samuel Alito “warned against any potential congressional action to defund the Supreme Court as he defended the importance of an independent judiciary,” according to The Hill. “Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities,” he stated. “So, it is important to preserve the independence of the judiciary. If that is eliminated, then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.” He also described the judicial branch as “the least powerful branch,” adding that “it is ‘vulnerable’ to Congress and the executive.” But that doesn’t mean judges can’t go too far, Alito added. “If you think about a hand grenade, a 500-pound bomb and a nuclear weapon,” he said, “the hand grenade is the least dangerous. But that is not to say that it is not dangerous.”.

    In February, “the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Donald Trump imposed last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act,” holding that the law does not grant the president the power to impose tariffs. The next month, the U.S. Court of International Trade “ordered Customs and Border Patrol to problem refunds to importers totaling about $166 billion.” Now, seven Senate Democrats are asking the Federal Trade Commission “to investigate whether large corporations that received billions of dollars in tariff refunds violated federal law by not passing them on to their customers,” according to USA Today. “By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs,” the senators wrote, “corporations may be in violation of the” Federal Trade Commission Act, which “empowers the commission to prevent ‘unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.’”.

    Industry observers note that during a Thursday panel at the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Convention, “White House counsel Will Scharf praised the Supreme Court’s June decision strengthening presidential firing power as a ‘generational win’” that “righted what he viewed as a ‘historic constitutional wrong,’” according to The Hill. “A president who can’t control who’s exercising the executive power that is vested in him, that’s a cabined presidency,” Scharf mentioned. “The Supreme Court did a masterful job,” he added. “Really got it right.”.

    On Thursday, former death row inmate Richard Glossip appeared in Oklahoma County District Court “for what was supposed to be his second hearing on pretrial motions” in the state’s effort to retry him for the 1997 murder of Barry Van Treese. “However, the hearing took a turn when the state announced an agreement between the prosecution and the defense,” under which “Glossip pleaded guilty to one count of accessory to murder,” according to KOKH in Oklahoma City. The plea agreement comes after the Supreme Court in 2025 “threw out Glossip’s murder conviction and death sentence,” determining that prosecutors had failed to correct false testimony. “Glossip’s sentencing is set for Dec. 17 and Dec. 18.”.

    Adam Liptak, The New York Times.

    Recent findings suggest that in his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak highlighted “hurdles and roadblocks [] erected by the Supreme Court” that may stand in the way of at least some of the new Congress’ planned investigations into “the Trump administration and its allies.” For example, in 2024’s Trump v. United States, in which the court granted the president “substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.” “Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding ‘which crimes to investigate and prosecute.’” It is also significant, according to Liptak, that “the court has never definitively resolved” whether Congress can “sue the executive branch,” an matter that will likely arise if the administration refuses “to give Congress documents or let officials testify.” Liptak noted that “it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate” disputes between Congress and the executive branch over access to information, “or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.”.

    In a recent development, during the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats in cases on birthright citizenship, tariffs, and his effort to fire Lisa Cook. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those issues.

    In his Nuts and Bolts column, Stephen Wermiel explored how the Supreme Court decides what cases to decide, also known as the certiorari or “cert.” process. According to him, “questions will continue to arise about how th[is] process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in a column for SCOTUSblog, Deborah Hellman and Lily Hu revisited the Supreme Court’s decision to grant review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on the circumstances under which facially neutral admissions policies violate equal protection by producing a discriminatory effect.

    In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored 11 petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices during today’s conference, which cover such issues as the Trump administration’s effort to remove certain noncitizens from the country without first allowing them to apply for asylum and a ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    In his Born Free and Equal column on Wednesday, Steven Calabresi reviewed Justice Samuel Alito’s newly introduced book and commended it as “exceptionally intellectual and provocative.” “The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not,” Calabresi concluded.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Amy reported that the Trump administration has once again asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to build a new White House ballroom. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    In her inaugural Substance and Procedure column on Monday, Rachel Bayefsky explored the Supreme Court’s application of a “history-and-tradition” analysis in recent cases on the constitutionality of agency adjudication – that is, “the practice of resolving disputes ‘in-house’ within administrative agencies instead of addressing” them in a court. According to Bayefsky, the court’s decision in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards “may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.”.

    According to recent reports, sarah Isgur and David French analyze free speech issues from the past three election cycles, including Donald Trump’s “they/them” ad in 2024 and the Trump administration’s threats to social media companies. They then discuss a free speech fight that may define the next two years.

    The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Samuel Nelson, who served on the court from 1845 to 1872.

    While you might think there’s only one justice with the name Samuel based on recent news coverage, there have actually been five with that first name in the court’s history – and in today’s justice biography, we’ll take a look at the second. (The first, if you recall, didn’t get things off to a particularly great start: He is the only justice to have been impeached.).

    Although referred to as “one of those nineteenth-century justices of whom we often lose sight” (the Journal of Supreme Court History said it, not us), Justice Samuel Nelson served on the court for 27 years as a “pragmatic yet low-key man,” as described by Oyez. Things began for him in Hebron, New York, where he was born in November 1792 to Scot-Irish farmers. His father helped pay Nelson’s Middlebury College tuition by selling a person who was enslaved. Nelson graduated from Middlebury in 1813; clerked at a Salem law firm; followed one of its partners to Madison County, New York when the firm split; and was admitted to the bar in 1817 (two years later, he married his law firm practice partner’s daughter).

    In 1820, Nelson was appointed the town’s postmaster and served as a presidential elector for James Monroe. He became a delegate to the 1821 state constitutional convention, where he pushed to eliminate property requirements for male voters.

    New York Gov. Joseph Yates appointed Nelson as a state circuit judge in 1823. Gov. Enos Throop elevated him to the New York Supreme Court of Judicature (that state’s highest trial court) in 1831, and he became its chief justice in 1837. In Jack v. Martin, he held that New York could not interfere with enforcement of the federal Fugitive Slave Act and noted that anyone who seized a free man would, under state law, “be answerable like any other trespasser or kidnapper.”.

    In a recent development, in 1845, Nelson ran for the U.S. Senate and lost. Shortly after, President John Tyler nominated him to succeed Justice Smith Thompson. The Senate confirmed Nelson by voice vote in February 1845, and he served as circuit justice for the 2nd Circuit (Connecticut, New York, and Vermont) while on the Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, on the bench, Nelson “kept a low profile,” generally voting with the majority. He did write a few notable decisions, one of them in 1850’s Hotchkiss v. Greenwood, a landmark patent law case. In 1857’s Fellows v. Blacksmith, Nelson wrote for a unanimous court that a land firm could not forcibly evict the Tonawanda Senecas, calling such litigation “appalling.” According to one scholar, Nelson “persuaded all his brethren, including those who had supported Jacksonian Indian removal policies, of the merits of the Tonawandas’ Seneca treaty arguments.” The same scholar wrote that Fellows eventually allowed for the treaty that let the tribe buy back 7,500 acres of its reservation.

    Fellows was decided the same year as Dred Scott v. Sandford. Nelson reportedly resisted behind-the-scenes pressure from incoming President James Buchanan to endorse at least part of Chief Justice Roger Taney’s opinion (unlike Justice Robert Grier). Nevertheless, he concurred with the majority, and scholars have “castigat[ed] him, along with Justice Robert Grier of Pennsylvania, for being the only two Northern jurists on the bench who voted with the majority in the case.” (Ten years later in Georgia v. Stanton, Nelson refused to let Georgia block Congress’ Reconstruction program, holding that its claims “call for the judgment of the court upon political questions.”).

    In the lead-up to the Civil War, Nelson and Justice John Campbell acted as intermediaries between Secretary of State William Seward and Southern commissioners who wanted the Confederacy recognized. Privately, Nelson wrote on Christmas Day in 1860 that “we almost despair of the republic” and in 1862 wrote to Justice Benjamin Curtis that he hoped the country might survive both “the fierceness of the enemy without and imbecility of the authorities within.”.

    Sources indicate that nelson also dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not legally blockade Southern ports until Congress declared war. The dissent (along with his vote in Ex parte Milligan to overturn the conviction of a man charged with helping the Confederacy and opposing expanding federal power) led critics to question his loyalty to the Union.

    Recent findings suggest that following the civil war, President Ulysses S. Grant in 1871 named the 79-year-old Nelson one of five American members of the commission handling claims against Great Britain for the damages caused by British-built Confederate ships, which Nelson accepted (although he wrote that he was “hardly at liberty to refuse”). The proceedings won the United States $15.5 million.

    Recent findings suggest that nelson retired in November 1872. He died in Cooperstown, Latest York, in December 1873, at age 81. One historian wrote that Nelson was a “quietly competent jurist” in comparison to several of “his more flamboyant and controversial judicial brethren” (some of whom we will be covering soon).

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 10, Judge Richard Posner passed away at the age of 87. Posner, who served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit from 1981 to 2017, was one of the most influential jurists never to have served on the Supreme Court. In addition to his voluminous opinions (some affirmed, others denied), Posner authored over 60 books and more than 500 articles and served as a Senior Lecturer in Law at the University of Chicago Law School. Among his many contributions, Posner helped give life to the law and economics movement and to the study of judging as an empirical pursuit. As Zach, our executive editor, can attest to first-hand, he was both charming and hilarious in person and did not suffer bad ideas lightly. But this is SCOTUSblog.
