    #90459. Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

    Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival.
    • Based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama.
    • The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival. Since then, Zvyagintsev has directed five more films, two of which—Leviathan (2014) and Loveless (2017)—were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. His most recent feature, Minotaur (2026), which is set against the backdrop of mobilization for the war in Ukraine, won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.

    Based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama. Successful businessman Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) suspects his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) of having an affair. Their son, Seryozha, is being bullied at school, and the mayor of the fictional Russian city where the film is set, demands that business owners provide him with a list of employees to be conscripted as soldiers—essentially, cannon fodder.

    The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.

    It has been revealed that zvyagintsev lives in France and is at the moment at work on a new film (that I thought was called Jupiter—more details below) about a Russian oligarch. We spoke on Zoom via a translator. The interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

    A heads up: possible spoilers in the discussion.

    According to recent reports, radha Vatsal: I want to start with some general observations: that fathers, wealth or power, and violence, often in the form of unexpected deaths, seem to be a theme that crop up frequently in your films. But there’s also a mythical dimension that we’ve seen in some of the titles like Minotaur and Leviathan, and I’m curious what draws you to this mythical element.

    Andrey Zvyagintsev: Only two out of six films have a mythological reference—Leviathan and Minotaur. Only two.

    AZ: Jupiter, no, it’s a working title.

    RV: Okay. All right, so then maybe–.

    In a recent development, AZ: Jupiter is a name we no longer aim to use because in the Venice Film Festival this year, there was a film named Jupiter. So we could no longer use that name. They did it faster than we could.

    In a recent development, [But to answer your question,] Minotaur, the film, has two sides to it. One is a personal family story, and the other is a story about society. So we could say that there are two films inside Minotaur, and they both have a very strong connection to each other. And they are represented in the title “Minotaur.”.

    Well, the first one, as you know from Greek mythology, is the mythological monster that lives in the labyrinth and demands human sacrifices. And then the other part, the more intimate family side—Balzac has a work called “The Physiology of Marriage” [1829] and the subtitle is “Meditations.” The interesting thing is that Balzac was twenty-five when he wrote that work. He was a very, very young man, and it’s really astonishing that someone so young has such an insight into family and married life.

    According to recent reports, there is a part where Balzac writes that marital life is like a labyrinth, where the husband wanders in anxiety and watches over his wife. And the husband experiences anxiety when he sees ambiguity, secrets, something unknown in the wife, and he waits anxiously in case there might be a lover around the corner of the labyrinth.

    Industry observers note that and there is a phrase that Balzac writes, and I’m going to try to quote it to you: That while the husband is wandering around the labyrinth, he’s waiting for the lover to jump out from around the corner; and the lover “minotaurizes”—so making minotaur into a verb—the husband. “Minotaurizes”—that’s the word Balzac uses.

    The metaphor is quite simple because for Balzac to give the husband horns, as the minotaur has horns, means to cheat on the husband. But I think it’s also interesting that we do not know what this encounter will entail, and the lover may very well be also the victim of the situation.

    So to go back to your question, the title works in two respects and has two sides and explanations to it.

    Recent findings suggest that RV: I wanted to discuss the use of interior space in Minotaur. I was very struck by the house. Like the apartment in Elena [Zyvagintsev’s domestic/crime drama from 2011], Gleb and Galina’s home feels like its own character in the film. And there’s a lot of glass and expensive surfaces. It’s also very restrained and tasteful, and it doesn’t match up to the idea we have in the west of new money in Russia being very flashy and in your face.

    So I was wondering if you could talk about how you center their home, and also your choice of the décor in their home and the restraint.

    AZ: I can tell you that upcoming money—especially the Russians, you can obviously find some crazy mansions and different manifestations of wealth. Much more ostentatious. This house is probably worth $2 to $3 million, which is not a lot of money for a really wealthy Russian businessman.

    According to recent reports, it was incredibly lucky to encounter a house like this in Riga, in Latvia, where we were shooting, because most houses there have this very European kind of look to them, which is not the style of houses you can find in Russia. And so this house was definitely an exception, and we were lucky to find it.

    And in the case of Elena, both Elena’s apartment with Vladimir, her husband, and the apartment where her son Seryozha lives with his family—it was all built for the film. In the case of the house you see in Minotaur, this is a house that belongs to the architect who built it, and he actually lives in it. And the only set that was built for Minotaur is the apartment of Anton, the lover. That’s a studio apartment that was built specifically for the film.

    In a recent development, RV: The extended sequence of violence that takes place halfway through the film, without any dialogue, is so engrossing. And I was wondering whether that whole sequence was planned or was some of it improvised? It feels like it takes place in real time.

    It has been revealed that AZ: It was not improvised at all. It was fully planned beat by beat because every scene that involves blood is automatically very hard to do because you have to wash the blood away after every take and then re-spill it. So it takes a lot of time and effort to do that.

    Industry observers note that so, as I said, we planned everything well in advance and in a very detailed manner. And we spent five days shooting at the apartment. So day one was love scenes between Galina and her lover. The second day was the encounter between the lover and the husband; and then days three, four, five were all dedicated to the murder scene and the aftermath. So we gave our guy one day to enjoy love, and then the other days, he was getting murdered.

    RV: Gleb’s advice to Seryozha when Seryozha tells him that he’s being bullied at school. I expected Glib to be more brutal, and I was surprised that he gave him quite mild advice of how to deal with the bullies.

    AZ: You seem to be the only person to think it was mild advice. Where are you from?

    RV: India, but I live in New York.

    Sources indicate that AZ:  Russia is a very patriarchal country, and this is how it happens there. The man is the head of the family. And some 100 years ago, children were not even allowed to start eating before the father starts. And if they did, they could be struck with a wooden spoon on their forehead. So this is regarded by many as a normal form of communication between father and children in Russia.

    And, this is an notable detail: Gleb starts with saying you have to grab [the bully] by the collar, but then he claims, do not touch him, but just say with the same expression, tell him very deliberately, if you do something like this one more time… So the advice has two parts to it.

    Industry observers note that I’m not entirely sure what the tool is against bullying at school and the way children sometimes relate to each other in an angry or violent manner. It’s a difficult conversation. So, it’s hard to tell what the right reaction would be.

    Sources indicate that this situation is very strange for me. If you have better advice on what to do if a child is getting bullied at school, I would love to hear it because I have a teenage son who is at school in France, in a boarding school, and he also had a problem with bullying, and I also had to give him some advice. My advice was more delicate, but I did explain to him that you have to face the person who tries to bully you and, you know, at least have a conversation.

    And going back to your first question about my titles having a mythological connotation, I made a joke earlier about Venice, you know, having a film in competition that was named Jupiter.

    But the truth is, I thought to myself that I probably have a few too many mythological titles. So my new film will be called something else, which I cannot tell you right now, but it will be something much better and much more interesting.

    It has been revealed that RV: Thank you very much. I look forward to seeing it.

    It has been revealed that radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The New York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums.
    • He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc.
    • Industry observers note that diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

    He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

    Industry observers note that diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:.

    A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

    Despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

    Recent findings suggest that hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

    Recent findings suggest that like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

    Sources indicate that john Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in upcoming crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

    Recent findings suggest that robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the substantial screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

    The Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

    Danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on Fresh Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

    In a recent development, the movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

    Sources indicate that dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a New York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

    • Recent findings suggest that before the court is a petition to review the U.S.
    • Though the pipeline manufacturer is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that one of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock), Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “atmosphere” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

    Recent findings suggest that before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline company. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

    Though the pipeline manufacturer is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in Oneida County v. Oneida Indian Nation, which held that there is a federal common law cause of action allowing Indigenous property owners to bring trespass actions in federal court.

    In a recent development, the Andeavor case has been accompanied in recent years by a slate of lower court decisions similarly diminishing Indigenous property rights. In Davilla v. Enable Midstream Partners, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit held that a pipeline trespasser on Indigenous property would not be ordered to remove the pipeline until the federal district court decided it was, among other things, in the “public interest” to do so. Under federal law, federal courts may not order injunctive relief unless such relief is in the public interest. The 10th Circuit’s decision imposed a public interest standard on Indigenous property when, arguably, it would not have done so in relation to private property.

    According to recent reports, similarly, a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin held in Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe Indians v. Enbridge Inc. that the tribe was not entitled to the immediate removal of a trespassing pipeline because the public interest favored its continued operation. Fortunately, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit reversed that decision. Other federal courts have also ordered immediate eviction of trespassers to Indigenous lands (e.g., United States v. Osage Wind), but the judiciary tends to invoke the public interest when favoring pipeline or other petroleum industry companies.

    Recent findings suggest that newland argues that some judges may be channeling a long tradition where the federal government assumed that Indigenous property is public property: Most pipelines running through Indigenous lands now originated in an earlier era where the federal government assumed a kind of guardianship over tribal nations, where the Interior Department granted easements and rights-of-way over Indigenous lands without tribal consent. For example, the Supreme Court once held that the secretary of the Interior was empowered to matter leases to natural resources extraction companies even over tribal opposition (Cherokee Nation v. Hitchcock).

    The tradition of guardianship arose in early Supreme Court decisions comparing the federal-tribal relationship to a “guardian-ward” relationship (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia). Congress did not enact laws generally asserting actual guardianship over tribal nations; instead, the relationship was more accurately characterized as a trust relationship, with federal government owning and managing tribal and individual Indian asserts in trust.

    Industry observers note that A trust beneficiary has legal rights that a ward does not. A ward does not possess the legal capacity to make their own decisions, while tribal nations and tribal citizens do. When federal or state actors did assert guardianship over Indigenous assets, tragedy often followed, as evidenced in the early 20th century killings of Osage people fictionalized in the film “Killers of the Flower Moon” or in the flooding of several Indian reservations in the mid-20th century by federal hydroelectric dam projects.

    In a recent development, often, when tribal nations attempted to assert their own legal rights, the judiciary allowed the federal government to block those efforts. Justice Neil Gorsuch recently raised this matter in his dissent in Arizona v. Navajo Nation, where he pointed out that, decades ago, the federal government blocked the Navajo Nation from asserting their water rights, which remain unsettled to this day. In those older cases, the fact that the federal government could stand in the shoes of Indigenous interests suggested that Indigenous property was therefore, in effect, public property.

    The Department of Justice’s litigation positions also frequently hearken back to expansive federal controls over Indigenous property. While the Supreme Court has explicitly overturned the earlier cases analogizing the federal-tribal relationship as a guardianship in cases such as United States v. Sioux Nation, DOJ attorneys are known to continue to assert guardianship-type control over Indigenous property. Indeed, federal judges have sanctioned them for making such claims post-Sioux Nation.

    Industry observers note that this legacy of guardianship once again has raised its head. D.C. Circuit briefing has concluded in a claim brought by the Tohono O’Odham Nation against the Department of Homeland Security regarding the administration’s strategy to build a border wall on the tribe’s land. The tribe argues that the federal common law cause of action recognized in Oneida undergirds the suit. In response, the DOJ now asserts that tribal nations may not sue the United States for trespass on hands held in trust by the federal government for the benefit of a tribal nation. This claim rings again of guardianship, where a ward normally does not have the legal capacity to sue their guardian.

    The import of the government’s claim in the border wall case, like the trespass action in Andeavor, has enormous consequences for Indian country: If the government can confiscate Indigenous property held in trust by the United States, then the judiciary will have allowed the federal government to reassume a guardianship-type relationship regardless of tribal consent or the federal government’s trust duties.

    According to recent reports, matthew L.M. Fletcher is the Harry Burns Hutchins Collegiate Professor of Law at the University of Michigan Law School.

    The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally.
    • That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series.
    • Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every great detective needs a Watson.

    Sources indicate that I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally. By “Watson,” I refer to the archetype of the Very Impressed Best Friend And Narrator. A hype man who also tells the story. A deputy who keeps going “wow, look at this guy” as he tells you about this guy. Bonus points if he’s also this guy’s roommate.

    That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series. He’s a carnival barker and a nonfiction writer. Sherlock Holmes is not only his friend, he’s his subject. Watson isn’t only HIS best friend, he’s his audience. But he’s also his publicist. He‘s fascinated by Holmes, and he knows tons of people will also be fascinated by Holmes. His job is PR, and man does he do it well.

    Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.

    Watson: Archie Goodwin  Detective: Nero Wolfe.

    In the beloved Rex Stout series, the young Archie Goodwin narrates AND does all the legwork for the affluent, grouchy, high-on-the-horse bibliophile and private detective Nero Wolfe who hates leaving his luxurious brownstone. Archie, a handsome and dapper young man, is a quick-witted, fast-talking factotum. And he’s always pretty impressed with the mental calculations of his sedentary boss.

    Sources indicate that watson: S.S. Van Dine Detective: Philo Vance.

    Recent findings suggest that S.S. Van Dine takes the Watson gambit even further than Watson does. He is a real person, the real-life writer of the Philo Vance books (though “S.S. Van Dine was a pen name; his real name was Willard Huntington Wright), who writes himself into the stories as the best friend of the brilliant, suave, dandyish detective Philo Vance. Here, he’s not Vance’s creator, merely his chronicler, and the two solve innumerable mysteries together during the Jazz Age.

    Watson: Unnamed  Detective: C. Auguste Dupin.

    We don’t know the name of the guy who narrates his friend and roommate Auguste Dupin’s feats of investigation, but he is really the OG Watson. They meet at various rare booksellers and eventually hit it off, becoming pals and then deciding to move in together.

    Watson: Capt. Arthur Hastings  Detective: Hercule Poirot.

    Sources indicate that hercule Poirot’s best friend Arthur Hastings doesn’t narrate ALL the Poirot stories (he narrates eight of thirty-three novels, and twenty-one of fifty-one short stories), because, after Hastings meets a beautiful music hall performer half his age in Murder on the Links, he marries her and eventually moves with her to South America, where they have four kids. But Hastings appears sprinkled throughout the Poirot canon, because he returns to England for business a lot. So they get together and crime-solve then.

    Watson: Anthony Horowitz Detective: Daniel Hawthorne.

    Sources indicate that look, I’d have such a soft spot for Anthony Horowitz even WITHOUT the these books, simply because I grew up reading the Alex Rider series. But the Horowitz and Hawthorne mysteries, in which “Horowitz himself” tags along as the sidekick and narrator (he’s NOT ONLY the Watson, here, but Van Dine). Their work is very collaborative (and these books are sneaky, since Hawthorne isn’t the real mastermind, but Horowitz himself).

    • According to recent reports, as the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it.
    • It has been revealed that just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases.
    • Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    According to recent reports, as the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it. There are key disputes tied to climate change, immigration, and the Second Amendment. But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs, birthright citizenship, executive authority, and the Voting Rights Act.

    It has been revealed that just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases. Perhaps of even greater note, though, is that it’s short on cases in general, as the court is running behind its typical pace for grants.

    The Fourth District Court of Appeal in Florida on Wednesday banned a disbarred Florida attorney convicted of fraud from submitting pro se filings in his case after he allegedly “flooded” a trial court with documents, many generated with artificial intelligence.

    After Willie Joe Jones of Florida filed more than 70 documents with a circuit court since April 2025, a panel of judges ordered the clerk of the court to reject any of his future filings unless they are signed by a lawyer in good standing with the Florida Bar.

    “Abusive AI filing poses a serious threat to the orderly administration of justice,” the panel wrote.

    #90445. Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1544 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border.
    • The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.
    • Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

    The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

    Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

    The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be swiftly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

    Recent findings suggest that the challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

    U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

    A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

    Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”.

    Industry observers note that the D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

    Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most important and effective pieces of the President’s response.”.

    Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he said, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”.

    Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”.

    And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent intends to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”.

    Sources indicate that the challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a fresh removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”.

    The statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”.

    The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they said, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

    The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

    Sources indicate that the court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services manufacturer violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

    The organization asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

    Sources indicate that the investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors said, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”.

    In a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the organization’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”.

    The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #90441. “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1351 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • Industry observers note that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • It has been revealed that in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move rapidly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he mentioned, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    Industry observers note that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito noted but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    It has been revealed that in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    Sources indicate that for most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Industry observers note that against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    The court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    Industry observers note that but I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    It has been revealed that another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    According to recent reports, that leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    Alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    Recent findings suggest that as I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    According to recent reports, the administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    Pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    It has been revealed that the 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    The new term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    It has been revealed that alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the new term.

    In a recent development, the 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    Recent findings suggest that so Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the glitch-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    Industry observers note that dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    #90439. Breaking: Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1863 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • Industry observers note that in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • It has been revealed that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    Industry observers note that in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    It has been revealed that A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    In a recent development, originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    In a recent development, for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    Similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s Newly introduced York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    Sources indicate that for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual people of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    Industry observers note that this criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    In a recent development, second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Finally, and most key in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Sources indicate that sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    According to recent reports, sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    According to recent reports, recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    According to recent reports, bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Recent findings suggest that many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    According to recent reports, from an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Sources indicate that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky states, courts must decide: which tradition?

    The existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at problem in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (33 w)

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.
    • According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, new research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images).

    New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

    According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

    Among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that indicated signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

    Recent findings suggest that researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They said AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

    “The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

    Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
